meta.name: Puli
meta.excerpt: The Puli is Hungary's iconic corded herding dog, with a unique coat that forms naturally into long, tight cords over two years. Athletic, energetic, and sharp-minded, the Puli is one of the most striking and capable herding breeds in the world.
meta.meta_description: Puli breed guide: corded coat care, formation timeline, temperament, and costs. Hungary's iconic herding dog with the remarkable natural corded coat.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: Hungary's Dancing Mop: The Corded Herder
intro.html:
The Puli is one of the most visually extraordinary dogs in the world. Its coat — a dense, naturally corded mass that hangs from the dog's body in long, rope-like locks — is unique among herding breeds and immediately recognizable to anyone who has seen one. But the Puli is far more than a remarkable coat. Beneath those cords is a compact, athletic, highly intelligent herding dog that has been working Hungary's great plains (the Puszta) for over a thousand years, managing flocks with a combination of speed, agility, and sharp thinking.

The Puli was brought to Hungary by the Magyar people during their migration from central Asia around 900 CE, and the breed has been integral to Hungarian pastoral culture ever since. The traditional herding system used different Puli types for different jobs — smaller dogs for agile, quick management of the flock on the move, and larger dogs for heavier work. Today's Puli represents the medium-sized variety that became the standard.

The coat is the Puli's most defining and most demanding characteristic. The cords form naturally from the interaction of the soft undercoat and the coarser outer coat, beginning in puppyhood and reaching full length by about two years of age. During the cord formation process, the owner must regularly separate the developing cords by hand to prevent them from matting together into unwanted flat masses. Once fully formed, the cords are relatively self-maintaining but require significant bathing effort — a fully corded Puli takes hours to wash and dry completely. The cords are waterproof and weather-resistant but can hold water for extended periods after bathing, making thorough drying an absolute necessity to prevent mildew and skin issues.

The Puli is an energetic, athletic, and clever dog. It jumps, climbs, and moves with remarkable agility for a corded dog. It is alert, quick-learning, and fully capable of herding and dog sports. It is also assertive and independent in the way of most herding breeds, requiring an experienced owner who can provide clear structure and adequate activity.

appearance.label: Appearance
appearance.heading: Unmistakable: Cords From Head to Tail
appearance.html:
A fully corded adult Puli is one of the most striking sights in the dog world. The cords hang from all parts of the body — head, body, legs, and tail — in long, flat-to-round rope-like locks that completely obscure the dog's underlying structure. The face is covered in cords that fan out from the head, hiding the eyes; the body cords hang to the ground on an adult dog. The tail's cords blend into the back cords when the tail is held over the back in typical spitz fashion.

Beneath the cords, the Puli is a compact, square-bodied dog of medium size. The body is muscular and well-proportioned, with a level back and well-angulated hindquarters. Height is 16–17 inches; weight 25–35 pounds. The most common color is solid black — this is the iconic Puli color — but the breed also comes in rusty black, gray (various shades), and white. White Pulik (plural of Puli) in particular are striking in their fully corded coats.

temperament.label: Temperament
temperament.heading: Energetic, Smart, and Devoted
temperament.html:
The Puli is an energetic, intelligent, and self-confident herding breed. It is devoted to its family and typically good with children it knows and other dogs it has been socialized with. The breed retains strong herding instincts — it may attempt to herd children, other pets, or moving objects, which is usually harmless but can be persistent. Early socialization and consistent training channel these instincts appropriately.

The Puli is not a passive companion. It is alert, perceptive, and has opinions that it expresses — vocally, physically, and behaviorally. It needs daily vigorous exercise, mental engagement through training or dog sports, and an owner who provides clear, consistent structure. The breed is playful and athletic, excelling at agility and herding sports, and genuinely enjoys games and interactive activities with its owner.

With strangers, the Puli is often initially cautious or reserved — appropriate watchfulness for a working breed. With proper socialization this caution is appropriate rather than reactive. The breed is not typically aggressive, but it is confident and will not back down from perceived challenges.

mikes_take.label: Mike's Take
mikes_take.heading: The Most Commitment-Intensive Coat in Herding
mikes_take.html: The Puli is a magnificent dog, and I mean that unreservedly. But I want to be honest about the coat, because most people who are drawn to the breed by pictures don't fully grasp what they're signing up for. Forming and maintaining cords is not grooming in the conventional sense — it's an ongoing project. During cord formation in the first two years, you're separating cords regularly by hand. Once formed, bathing a fully corded adult Puli takes the better part of a day when you include drying time. This is not a breed for someone who wants minimal grooming. But if you embrace it — if the coat is part of why you love the breed — the Puli rewards you with a dog of tremendous athletic ability, sharp intelligence, and real personality. It's not for everyone. For the right person, it's extraordinary.

care.label: Care
care.heading: Vigorous Exercise and Specialized Coat Management
care.html:
The Puli needs at least 60 minutes of vigorous exercise daily. It is a high-energy herding dog that excels at agility, herding, and obedience sports. Mental stimulation is equally important — without it, the Puli's intelligence finds its own outlets. Training should be consistent and ongoing, using positive reinforcement; the breed responds well to reward-based methods and has the intelligence to learn complex behaviors.

Coat care is the most time-intensive aspect of Puli ownership. During cord formation (approximately 9 months to 2 years of age), cords must be separated by hand regularly — weekly or more — to prevent them from matting together. Once fully formed, cords require inspection and separation at the base monthly to catch any new fusion. Bathing a fully corded Puli requires soaking the cords through completely (which takes time given their thickness), thorough rinsing, and then drying — which can take 8–12 hours with a dryer, or much longer air-drying. Incomplete drying causes mildew and skin issues. Many corded Puli owners plan bath days around clear, warm weather or use high-velocity dryers.

Some owners choose to keep their Puli in a brushed (non-corded) coat, which requires regular brushing but eliminates the cord management and long drying times. This is a valid choice for pet owners not interested in the full corded coat.

health.label: Health
health.heading: Generally Robust with Some Hereditary Concerns
health.html: The Puli is a generally healthy and long-lived breed for its size, with a lifespan of 10–15 years. The primary hereditary concerns are hip dysplasia, progressive retinal atrophy, and eye conditions. OFA hip certification and CAER eye exams are recommended screening tools for responsible breeding. The Puli's skin can be susceptible to conditions if the coat is not properly dried after bathing — mildew and fungal skin infections can develop under inadequately dried cords. Keeping the coat clean and thoroughly dry after bathing is the primary skin health preventive measure.

cost.label: Cost
cost.heading: Moderate Acquisition Cost with High Time Investment
cost.html: Puli puppies from reputable breeders typically cost $1,200–$2,000. The primary cost of the corded coat is time rather than money — professional cord-knowledgeable groomers are rare and expensive if found. Most Puli owners learn to manage the cords themselves. Annual ongoing costs run $1,200–$2,200 for food and routine veterinary care of a medium-sized active dog.

right_for_you.label: Right for You?
right_for_you.heading: For Owners Who Embrace the Commitment
good_fit: Experienced dog owners who are specifically drawn to the breed's unique coat and working heritage and are fully prepared for the time investment of cord management and bathing
Owners who can match the breed's exercise and training needs
Households committed to early socialization and consistent boundaries
People who enjoy daily engagement and active companionship with their dog
Homes with the appropriate space and lifestyle for the breed's energy level
not_fit: You work full-time with 8+ hours away from home — Pulis need 90+ min of vigorous daily activity, and under-exercised dogs of this breed often develop destructive chewing, barking, or separation anxiety
You can't commit 15-30 minutes daily to brushing or budget $80-150/month for professional grooming — Puli coats matt fast without consistent care

finding.label: Finding a Puli
finding.heading: Puli Club of America and Reputable Breeders
finding.html:
The Puli Club of America (PCA) is the AKC parent club. Health testing should include OFA hip evaluation and CAER eye certification. The breed is uncommon in the United States and reputable breeders may have waitlists. Ask breeders specifically about cord formation guidance and whether they provide ongoing support to new owners learning to manage the cords.

faq.q: How long does it take for a Puli's cords to fully form?
faq.a: Approximately two years for full cord development, with cords beginning to form around 9 months of age. During this formation period, the owner must regularly separate developing cords by hand to prevent unwanted matting. Full-length cords on an adult dog reach the ground.

faq.q: Can a Puli be kept without cords?
faq.a: Yes. Some pet owners choose to brush out the coat rather than cord it. A brushed Puli still has a thick, full coat but without the distinctive rope-like locks, eliminating the cord management and the long drying times after bathing. The dog is the same regardless of coat management choice.

faq.q: How do you bathe a corded Puli?
faq.a: Bathing a fully corded Puli requires soaking the cords thoroughly (they resist water initially), lathering, and rinsing each cord clean. Drying takes 8–12 hours with a high-velocity dryer or significantly longer with air drying. The cords must be fully dry to the core to prevent mildew and skin infections. Most owners plan Puli bath days as dedicated projects.
